notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00429.opp-gr: Title: πρός is ambiguous here, and the title's relation to Antiochus is uncertain; the text of this stretch names neither Antiochus nor the baker. "Concerning" is a neutral rendering. Several places are damaged in the scan, and I supplied the sense: in 1.1, αὑτῶν μενοι is read as a participle such as ἡγούμενοι ("counting"), and τῶν των as τῶν τοιούτων ("such"); in 1.2, κόσιν is read as a form such as πιπράσκουσιν ("to the sellers"), and γοντες as λέγοντες; in 3.1, οὐ ροντες is read as οὐ χαίροντες ("not enjoy", with a threat implied; the fire is presumably arson); in 8.2, τὰ νου is read as something like "his" ("at his expense"), and πτῃ as κλέπτῃ ("thief"). In 7.1, a connective seems to have been lost between ἀνελόντος and δόντος. In 6.1, οὔδει is read as οὐδ' εἰ. In 10.1, Coccus is unidentified; he is presumably someone notorious for a beating or for cruelty. In 12.1, the sentence beginning "And when the man I had sent" breaks its construction in the Greek, and the English keeps that break. The last sentence of 12.2 is compressed and its exact sense is uncertain. The section numbers printed in the text are omitted.

15.3: the text at 'τῶν λεγόντων] ἐχόντων' is disturbed, with a stray bracket; I have taken it as 'the speakers having all the gods in every oath'. 20.3: 'του' is probably damaged; I read it as 'on this'. 23.1: 'δώσειν νῦν δίκην τοῦ μὴ ὅσην νῦν δίκην λαβεῖν' is awkward and may be corrupt, and the clause 'οὐδ' ὡς οὐ πολλαί, γνοὺς...' is compressed, so the rendering is uncertain. 24.1: the damaged word 'ματος' is read as ῥήματος ('word'), referring to νουθετῆσαι ('admonish'). 24.3: 'εἰσηχώς' is read as 'having brought before [him]'. Other broken words are supplied from evident readings: μηδενός in 15.2, τἀναντίον and νόμων in 29.1. ἀρτοπόπος and σιτοποιός are both rendered 'baker', in keeping with ἀρτοποιός.

§33: ἔλεγχος is rendered "exposure"; it may mean formal proof or conviction. §33, the sentence on the banker is compressed: it seems that the man who denied receiving the money from the banker had in fact received it but could not keep it, since he had to return it to the bank. §35: τούτοιν ("of these two") is taken as Augarus and his son.

nodes.text: On his own behalf, on account of the advocacy
concerning Antiochus.

The best men in the city, who stand furthest from envy and who, in benefactions to it, rejoice with both those who have received good and those who have done it, praise the help I gave the baker and agree that it has both justice and the common interest on its side; but others, [counting it] a loss to themselves if I should appear to have done something good, say that what was done is wicked and the sign of a wicked character. For my part, because I despise such people, I would have paid them no attention, but since my friends urge me to say something even now, I could not stay silent.

I shall say what all of you know, and about which no one would dare to say that I am lying. When the people, with unlawful uproar, had driven the shows from the stage and were causing fear of greater things, saying that the city was being wronged over bread, the governor, instead of checking this with threats, said that he would do everything they wanted and rose to leave; and the next day the boldness of the multitude brought matters to such a point that he legislated what was most pleasing to the many but had no possibility [of being carried out], and there was no small rush of men and women to whatever loaves appeared. Most went up [to the sellers] offering silver to buy, but on hearing that there was none, and seeing it for themselves at the same time, they went away doing and saying what is natural for those who think they are going to die.

The second day, and there were blows over the loaves, and those who could not buy were more than the one who could. The third, and the trouble was worse, so that as we were leaving after bathing the hungry followed us, saying that we would not enjoy our dinner, for there was fire. On the fourth day there was much talk in the agora that old men had died, that children had died. And I saw an old woman carrying a child and crying out this very thing, that unless someone gave it a share of bread it would die, and at the same time she held out the price.

The bread was fought over, and they shoved one another and in places even struck one another, and strength was then worth a great deal. The weaker man carried home not bread but wounds and torn clothing. This emptied the city of its councillors, and they were in the country, counting it a gain not to be burned along with their own houses; for that was what was expected.

In this storm one of the gods moves me, for the deed was certainly not mine, to say something to the governor about the calamity that had taken hold, and, carried in the hands of slaves, for my horse happened to be away, by rebuking at one moment, advising at another, frightening at another, and at some point even pleading, I barely drew him away from his great obstinacy over things impossible.

This, however, was not enough for the recovery; it was also necessary to bring the bakers down from the mountains and the caves in which they had hidden themselves. And this was not easy, since promises were distrusted and oaths were distrusted. But when I gave myself to the matter and spoke with them through those by whom it was possible, they considered that they had a trustworthy guarantor and at the same time said they remembered an old favour, when I snatched them from blows and torturers, without needing long speeches to the sensible Philagrius, since it was enough to shake my head as at harsh measures; in return for that, then, they said, there was nothing that they would not do, not even if they had to add the bodies of their children to the brushwood.

Having said such things they added the deed, and each came to such a pitch of eagerness that one night was enough for so great a change. It was not yet day, and everything was full of bread, so that loaves lay set out, and people walked past them, the abundance of them having removed the struggle over buying and given everyone confidence that whenever anyone came he could get some.

The kind of pleasure that people feel when they escape a shipwreck that was close at hand through the aid of the Tyndaridae, or that those shut in till then feel when a siege is lifted, such was ours when the agora returned to its former appearance, so that we embraced and kissed one another, now that the dangers from hunger had been cast out.

While the other gods and Fortune were being praised, along with the men who had served them, [the governor] put in charge of the sale of bread Candidus, the half-mad, believing that those whom he had prepared to make this announcement were the city. They were Candidus' own slaves and some others of those who had eaten at his expense. So Candidus, having found an opportunity profitable to a thief, was a bad guardian of what he had been entrusted with, and he gave away enemies to enemies, selling to their enemies those bakers who had given some offence, as happens among men in the same trade.

So, having arrested a man, a decent old man, living with his wife, raising children, milling no small amount of wheat every day into bread, and held in respect from every side among those of his trade, he slandered him, saying that he had done wrong over the bread. And having thrown the governor into anger with provoking words, he stripped the wretched man and flayed him before the eyes of his enemies. And the affair went to such an excess that Coccus seemed to be nothing.

But to Candidus this appeared a small thing, and he added the leading of the wretched man around through the whole city, both intensifying the harm from the blows by the postponement of medicines and inflicting a second penalty, that of shame. When the sun was near setting and he was about to be seen by his own neighbours at the hands of those leading him, his wife fell at their knees and begged them to grant him this favour at least, that his back be covered. They did not grant it as a favour, but they sold it. And a doctor was there, and there was fear for his life.

As this story was widespread, I sent someone to find out whether these things were so, and whether payment had been given for the man's getting a bed. And when the man I had sent came reporting both, how most unpleasantly I bathed, and could not eat dinner, and <spent the night> seeing the blows in my dreams, these things I shall pass over; but the tears of his wife at daybreak, who would not have pitied her, flung on the ground and beating her breast, asking for support in saying these things to the governor? I led her away from this, perhaps wrongly, in not letting her obtain as much redress as was deserved, and I directed her instead to the advocate of the city; for surely she ought not to be deprived of this consolation too. So I admit that I was present at the inquiry into these matters and that I contributed, not many, but nevertheless some words on the woman's behalf.

To the best men, then, as I said at the beginning, I seemed to have done something fine, but to those who burst [with envy] if anyone wins a good name for anything, something bad, novel, and not like me. But if what was done is just, and yet this is novel and not like me, they are saying nothing other than that I have reached old age while neglecting what is just. Yet who does not know that when I go through the city I never pass by anyone weeping, but I have stopped, felt pain, sought out the wrongdoer, and when I convicted him I imposed a penalty, and when I could not I was grieved? Many, too, who deserved a greater penalty have come under the advocates at my sending. For justice does not everywhere lie in preventing someone from suffering anything; what is sufficient in punishment also belongs to what is just.

As for outrages dared against myself, I know how not to take redress, but when another has suffered something I do not bear it. And if it is a fine thing never to have prosecuted anyone, here too I was not the accuser, but I pitied the isolation of the woman, whom love of her husband made an accuser, while her lack of allies persuaded me to help. For when would she have dared to break into speech, or to appear in public in the first place, had her fear not been taken away by what came from us? For she would never have gone unnoticed by those banded together with Candidus and would easily have been destroyed by them; knowing this well, she would have sat at home groaning.

So the courage of the wronged woman against those who wronged her has come to her from us. Yet even so someone, sitting with his own friends, has already called me a malicious meddler. How so, my dear man? For if the one who is angry with those who have done some evil could reasonably be called this, what shall we say those who did it ought to be called?

Now, that even if I had firmly resolved never in any way to touch any such matter, it was not possible to stand aside from this one once and for all, and that I would have been doing something reasonable even if I had brought a formal charge myself, one may learn from the following.

When that terrible time and the great fear drove the bakers up to the mountain peaks, and the one thing that seemed to me to bring safety was that they should come down and light their fires as before, but persuasion was to be had from nowhere, even though the speakers had all the gods in every kind of oath, then I alone was able to do this, since my words alone were thought free of suspicion.

And I would not say that I had been bound by a compact, that I would indeed help if any harm should come, as Achilles was by the seer; but this very fact, that they had asked for nothing of the kind, I thought should make me feel the obligation more than agreements made with the strongest pledges. Now the man who took the blows neither said, nor was going to say: "This, surely, is because of that man who, pleased with his success in persuading, neglects those he persuaded. Candidus is destroying us, and he knows and pays no heed."

So he refrained from [blaming] me even as he groaned, but I would have been ashamed both to be and to seem a traitor to the men through whom I had saved the city when it was already lost. For who should have been struck by what had happened before I was? Who should have felt pain? Who should have been indignant? What father? What mother? What brothers? What kin? The moment demanded my grief, my voice, my indignation; so that even if the man had been neglected by his wife, he would still have deserved to receive care from me, especially since, if I had not done this, I would have wronged myself as well as him. For how could I have gone to a temple? How could I have prayed? With what eyes could I have looked at the statues of the gods, conscious of so great an evil in myself? How would my whole past life not have been damaged for me by this one thing? Was I, then, bad in the very matter in which I feared being proved bad, and was I caught in what I most shunned? And what sense does that make?

Now the reckoning of what was just was enough to urge me to help the man who had suffered these terrible things, but as it was there was something else besides this that carried great compulsion. What was this? Fear of like evils. For if I had not then been angered by what was done, and had not done the things for which these people abuse me, and if everyone had known this, Candidus would have gone through all the bakers like a torrent, now imitating what he had done, now even outdoing it, and the mountains would have held them once more, and famine the city.

And perhaps Candidus would not even have got through them all with his beating; for once the first man had been left unprotected, each would have saved himself, his flight getting ahead of the outrage, and things would again have been as they were before, or even more terrible, there being no one to call them back to their work. For I myself would no longer have been trusted, since my earlier words would have been proved false by the same events.

Do my actions, then, deserve blame, and not rather words of praise, better than those now spoken? For if anyone were to examine it strictly, though I shrink from saying it, yet I am compelled to: I have twice saved this city, both restoring the bakers to it and retaining them, at one time persuading them to come down, at another preventing them from fleeing.

"For I was serving the governor's word," he says. And that word was to admonish the man for some offence concerning the loaves. I could have said something on this too, both that Candidus's accusation was greater than the deed, and that the weight of the loaves, just as it was less than it should be in some, so was more in others; but leaving this aside I shall come to the following point, whether anyone can cite a number of blows stated by the holder of office, as great as the number given, and as cruel as many have seen. Even in that case Candidus would certainly have done wrong in not being gentler than the man who had given the order, which we see even slaves doing for one another when one is handed over to another for a beating; and we see the very men who handed them over praising this, once their anger has subsided.

This I will not say to Candidus; rather, let this harshness be just, if he heard in express terms that Antiochus must suffer all that he has suffered. But he could not say so. Surely, then, he was clearly master at least of the lesser [penalty], and he was not going to pay any penalty for not exacting as great a penalty as he did now, nor was the governor going to ask the attendants, "How many were the blows?", nor, on learning that they were not many, to hurt Candidus by word or deed. And yet what prevented him, if he wished the blows to be so many, from stating the number, and that those striking must be among the more robust, such as the one Candidus set over him, his own son?

I am amazed that he did not feel shame even at the mildness of the word itself; for it was not the word of a man enraged or seething, but of one rather afraid that something violent might happen, and one that fathers have often used to a tutor on behalf of their children. But that great quantity of blood, and the skin cut through, and the exposed flesh, these were your work and that of your wickedness.

The governor himself makes clear, by what he did to another man, that these things were outside his own intention. For when the charge passed to another man, he took hold of the person of the one thought to have committed the offence and, imitating the gentler sort of schoolteachers, let him go, showing by what he did to the other what he would have done if someone had brought the first man before him too.

And what does more to refute Candidus's pretext: for looking to what, tell me, to what speech, to what word, to what syllable, to what nod, did you add those things far heavier than the blows? Among them were that the man was deprived of doctors and was made a pitiable spectacle for everyone in the city, driven along like one of the cattle. And if you claim that all this lies within the term "admonition", then even if you had clubbed the man to death you would, it seems to me, have taken refuge in the same word. But no one would have tolerated that either then or now. For it was neither the governor nor what he said that was destroying Antiochus, but the fact that money had been given against Antiochus by Antiochus's enemies, and that Antiochus's wife had been unable before the blows to give this man as much gold as he wanted; since even after the blows, though not so much, some was given all the same.

"So for Antiochus," someone will say, "you had to hurt Candidus, for the baker, one of the most distinguished men?" I was not unaware of the distance between the fortunes of the two, nor that the one owns a large house, while the other pays rent for the rooms in which he lives; nor that the one has much good land, while the other has a mill; nor that the one indulges his belly, while the other cannot; nor that the one is free to be idle, while the other must toil. I know this and many other things besides.

But I was not then putting Antiochus before Candidus, but the just before the unjust; for the one belonged to Antiochus, and the other was Candidus's. And no one, not even the most unjust of men, would dare to say that the place of justice does not command respect. For this reason, too, we see that those who leave unbribed courts victorious are not always the rich, but sometimes these, sometimes the poorer, as justice makes either side [the winner].

But you would be the sort of man to say to those judges too: "You have not acted well, sirs, in slighting the power of the man who lost before you and honouring the weakness of the man who won, when you could have done the opposite." And if you would not do this to a judge, why do it to me? For I, at any rate, think that everywhere justice ought to have great power. If this were so, human affairs would not fall so far short of divine ones as they do now. As it is, what above all makes our life bitter is this, that the written laws are many, some old, some new, but they are gleefully trampled on by wrongdoers, greed drawing them to itself more than these laws restrain them.

But neither at any other time have I ever abandoned the wronged to the wrongdoers because the latter were among the more illustrious and the former among the lowlier, nor was I going to let this happen to me now. For, let alone Candidus, not even my own father, had he done the same as Candidus, would I have put before the baker who suffered such things, nor before anyone else in a lesser trade, not, by the gods, before a cheese-seller or a vinegar-seller or a dried-fig seller or a cobbler. So let no one speak to me of chariots or athletes or bears or hunters; for justice, set against all these, persuades one to heed it rather than them.

And it persuades one also to bear what comes from the enmity to come. For that the man is hostile over these matters and will plot in every way and will not lack accomplices, I know very well. Yet not from fear of such a war would I have chosen both to be and to be thought a traitor to justice. For neither do we pardon those who desert their posts, even though we know that they commit this offence out of fear. For this is the very charge, that through fear they ruin what is their duty. For this reason they die shamefully, because they were unwilling [to die] honourably.

So it was honourable for me too to guard this post. For even if no one was going to indict me or judge me, still the gods would have blamed me for this, and I would have eaten myself up, knowing what wrong I had done. And what is more, I had hopes from the very act of doing what was just. For I believed that the gods, who praised what I myself praised, would also make me stronger than those who would make war on me. So let him gather whatever sort of band he wishes and can, and let him undermine me in secret and fight me in the open. For with the weight of the gods on our side, both he himself and those he collects will be a laughingstock.

"Why," he says, "did you prevent the penalty due upon the exposure?" Because, first, I considered the exposure itself no small penalty. Next, those who had been wronged themselves begged me to seek nothing further and not to rouse so large a body of soldiers to war against a workshop. So by the same reasoning by which I worked for the exposure, I worked for there being no punishment. For the former was the act of a man pitying the wronged, and the latter of one obliging those same people, especially since they were also able to recover what was theirs. For the man who denied having received [the money] from the banker, even though he had received it, had not got it. For he had to bring it back to the bank.

Thus in what I did and did not do I was not at war with myself. My critics, however, I could show to be at war with themselves, since they abuse me both for bringing the matter to trial and for being very eager that the soldier should not pay the penalty. For if they blame what came from anger, let them praise what came from clemency; and if they find fault with what came from clemency, why do they not credit my sharing the woman's anger to what is honourable?

And further I might add this to what has been said, that even if I had greatly desired the punishment, the wish of Augarus had to prevail, the soldier's brother, a friend and associate of ours, who has in our school a son who is not one of the many, but of those for whom one might even call the parents blessed in the fortune of their sons' nature. Of these two, then, the one said something about his brother, while the other said nothing, but by his silence did the same.

Many, many great things were saving the soldier. And I should like everyone to know this about me in general, that against those who do wrong and despise the laws I wage war until I have brought them down, but when I see them lying prostrate I make peace.
